group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old man presented to the ambulatory pre-operative clinic five days before an elective laparoscopic left inguinal hernia repair with mesh placement that the general surgery team anticipates will last 45–60 minutes under general anesthesia, require no bowel resection, and have an estimated blood loss of less than 50 mL with same-day discharge to home. He walked from the parking lot at a brisk pace while carrying his overnight bag, conversed comfortably during registration, and chose the stairs rather than the elevator to reach the second-floor examination area. At home he mows a quarter-acre lawn with a self-propelled mower, climbs two flights of stairs to his study several times daily, and regularly cycles ten miles on a rail-trail without chest discomfort, undue dyspnea, or palpitations. Eight years ago he awoke with substernal pressure radiating to the jaw; troponin I was elevated and coronary angiography showed a 95 % proximal right coronary artery stenosis that was treated with a drug-eluting stent. He completed cardiac rehabilitation, has experienced no recurrent angina, and follows up annually with cardiology; a resting echocardiogram performed six months ago demonstrated a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 55 % with no segmental wall-motion abnormality and only trivial mitral regurgitation. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg each morning, lisinopril 10 mg nightly, and high-intensity atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime; adherence is confirmed by pharmacy fill records and his own detailed medication log. Hypertension was first noted in his late forties and is well controlled on the medications already mentioned; home readings average 118–126/70–76 mm Hg. He denies diabetes, has never used insulin or any other glucose-lowering agent, and his most recent fasting plasma glucose was 94 mg/dL. Hyperlipidemia is managed with the statin above; his most recent LDL cholesterol was 62 mg/dL. He has never experienced transient monocular vision loss, limb weakness, speech disturbance, vertigo, or other neurologic symptoms suggestive of cerebrovascular events, and carotid imaging has never been indicated. Respiratory history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis; he has never smoked, drinks an occasional craft beer on weekends, and has no history of recreational drug use. Surgical history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy at age 22. Family history is notable for a father who underwent triple coronary bypass at 73 and a mother who died of breast cancer at 79; there are no premature cardiac or cerebrovascular deaths among first-degree relatives. Review of systems today is negative for fever, weight change, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, intermittent claudication, abdominal pain aside from the reducible groin bulge, nausea, or bleeding tendency. After five minutes seated, vital signs obtained in the right arm showed blood pressure 122/68 mm Hg, regular pulse 62 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 °C orally, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air; body mass index is 26 kg/m². He appears well nourished and in no distress. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is located in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 with no gallop, rub, or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with symmetric expansion. Abdomen is soft with a visible, reducible left inguinal bulge that protrudes on Valsalva; there is no organomegaly, ascites, or tenderness elsewhere. Extremities are warm with 2 + dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and no edema or cyanosis. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation to light touch, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 15.0 g/dL, hematocrit 45 %, white blood cells 6.4 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 220 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 0.82 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting lipid panel obtained in the same sample shows total cholesterol 142 mg/dL, HDL 48 mg/dL, and triglycerides 110 mg/dL; liver enzymes and international normalized ratio are within reference ranges. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed today shows normal sinus rhythm at 60 beats per minute with inferior Q waves consistent with prior infarction but no ST-segment deviation or T-wave inversion compared with a tracing from a year earlier. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph displays clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and no pulmonary vascular congestion. Airway assessment documents Mallampati class II visibility, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesiology plan is to continue beta-blocker, antihypertensive, and antiplatelet therapy the morning of surgery, administer a balanced general anesthetic with multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, employ goal-directed crystalloid guided by non-invasive cardiac output monitoring, and place sequential compression devices prior to induction. The patient demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding midnight fasting, medication timing, and postoperative activity expectations and voiced understanding of potential complications such as surgical site infection, urinary retention, anesthetic risks, and cardiac events; he expressed confidence in proceeding with the scheduled hernia repair in order to return to pain-free exercise and household duties.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: the planned elective inguinal hernia repair does not qualify → 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent counts despite the absence of current angina → 1.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical signs → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA → 0.
- Insulin-treated diabetes: no diabetes or insulin use → 0.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 0.82 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
